title: AI-Generated Content Must Be Clearly Labeled, Says EU
paragraphs: It is becoming harder and harder to tell whether a picture, video or piece of text was made by a person or by artificial intelligence. In the European Union, new rules now require some AI-generated content to be clearly labeled.
The rules are part of the EU's AI Act, a law that controls how AI is used in Europe. A section of the law called Article 50, which deals with transparency, began to apply on August 2, 2026.

Under the rules, there are two main groups that must follow them. The first group is the companies that make AI systems which create images, audio, video or text. They must mark this content in a way that computers can read, so that it can be identified as made by AI. The second group is the people and organizations that use AI to create content. They must clearly label deepfakes, which are realistic images, videos or audio of real people or events that are not real. In addition, they must label AI-generated text that is published to inform the public, unless a person has checked and edited it.

To help companies follow the law, the European Commission published a Code of Practice in June 2026. It recommends using several methods together, such as hidden information in files, called metadata, and watermarks. It also suggests using a common EU "AI" label, which must be clear and easy to see the first time people see the content. Following the code is voluntary, but companies that sign it can use it to show that they are obeying the law.

There are some exceptions. For example, the rules are more flexible for artistic, creative and fictional works. Companies that break the rules could be fined up to €15 million or 3% of their total yearly sales around the world. The rules also apply to companies outside the EU if their AI content is used in the EU.
However, some questions remain. For example, technology for detecting AI content is not yet considered reliable enough.
